blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Choose a whole-text structure that fits the category and the task; order material for effect; plan and write one continuous piece of 600–900 words.

blocks.heading: Whole-text structure
blocks.text: Whole-text structure is the shape of a piece from its opening to its ending: what it promises, how it develops, and how it closes. The shape is a decision, made before the writing starts, and the extended writing task — one continuous piece of 600–900 words in the category chosen from the paper’s selection, carrying twenty-five marks — is the task where the decision earns its keep.

blocks.heading: The shape each category tends to take
blocks.text: The shape each Section B category tends to take is different, and the plan starts from the category’s own shape. A story follows an arc: an opening situation, a conflict that complicates it, a turning point, and a resolution that shows what changed — the arc named in topic 2.3. A discursive piece explores: it opens the question, gives the sides their room, and reaches a reasoned view — the dialectic taught in topic 2.4. A review judges: it introduces what is reviewed, sets the criteria, weighs the evidence and lands the verdict — the shape taught in topic 2.5. One shape is not better than another; each is what its category’s reader arrives expecting.

blocks.heading: Planning the 600–900
blocks.text: Planning a 600–900-word piece runs in four steps. First fix the purpose and the audience, because the shape serves them. Then choose the shape: the arc, the exploration, the judgement — or a shape the task itself suggests. Then mark the sections: what each one does, in order, and where the turning point or verdict sits. Then give each section its share of the words — roughly 100 for an opening, 400 to 600 for the developing middle across two or three sections, and 100 for an ending that keeps its room.

blocks.heading: Chronological and thematic order
blocks.text: Chronological organisation follows time’s order: first this happened, then that. Thematic organisation follows the argument’s or the picture’s own logic: the cheapest objection first, the widest view last, the senses in the order a visitor would meet them. The choice is made for effect: a memoir of one day wants chronology, because the day’s shape is the story; a review of a course wants themes, because the reader deciding whether to enrol wants the teaching, the value and the verdict, not the Tuesday. Chronology is the habit; effect is the reason to keep it or break it.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a plan made in four steps
blocks.text: A task sets a description of a crowded place in the minutes before an event begins, with a focus on anticipation and the effect of tension built from calm rather than noise. The plan: purpose and audience — a general reader to be placed in the crowd; shape — a single scene built in waves, not a story; sections — the emptying last hour (100 words), the arrivals (200), the murmur building (200), the last minute (150), the moment itself withheld (50); shares — given, and the ending kept its room. Four steps, four minutes, and the writing that follows has somewhere to go.

blocks.heading: Worked example: withholding in a review
blocks.text: The review of a first-aid course holds its verdict to the last paragraph, and the holding is structural: the account, the criteria and the evaluation each end with the reader’s question still open — is it worth it? — so the verdict lands into a reader who has weighed the evidence themselves and is ready to be told. The same review with the verdict first would inform just as efficiently and persuade half as well, because a verdict before the evidence asks for trust and a verdict after it has earned the trust — which is why reviews are built back to front from their own conclusions.

blocks.heading: The ending, chosen
blocks.text: Ending on one image or line makes a piece memorable because memory keeps the last thing given: the closing choice is the piece’s parting gift, and it is chosen, not fallen into. The 600–900 range has a lower limit because development needs room: 600 words is where developed sections become possible, and writing short of it thins every section alike. Both facts bear on the same paragraph — the last one — which is why the plan reserves its hundred words before anything else spends them.

blocks.heading: The plan is the exam skill
blocks.text: Section B is worth twenty-five of Paper 2’s fifty marks, and it is the task most improved by planning and most damaged by its absence: a piece planned in four minutes has sections, shares and a kept ending, and a piece unplanned discovers its shape in the last hundred words, which is where the rushed ending comes from. Practise the plan until four minutes buys it — purpose, shape, sections, shares — and the writing time that follows is spent writing rather than deciding.

blocks.heading: Counterarguments placed, not appended
blocks.text: The discursive article about social media gives the friendships-have-thinned case its own full section, and the strongest version of it, before the reply — because a counterargument answered in a clause is a counterargument being hidden, and the reader knows it. Placing the objection beside the point — and answering it in the same room — lets the reader watch the argument survive its strongest test. Appended objections, dealt with in a sentence each at the end of a paragraph, read as decoration and convince no one who held them.

blocks.heading: Two failures of the whole
blocks.text: The first failure is the abrupt or rushed ending: the piece stops because the words ran out or the time did, and the resolution is compressed into a line or missing entirely — the reader is dropped where the piece should have landed them. The second is writing well short of 600 words, often because Section A took too long: the sections shrink, the development is the first casualty, and the ending is the second. Both failures share a cure, and it is the plan: a piece with its sections marked and its ending’s room kept does not run out of shape, because the shape was spent on purpose.
